abstract:
Author(s): Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, and Thomas E. Albrecht

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of the physics and chemistry of transplutonium elements under high pressure, focusing on their electronic structure and material properties.
motivation: Transplutonium materials are important for nuclear applications and exhibit unique electronic behavior, but their study under pressure is challenging due to radioactivity and complex electron correlations.
method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical work on metals, alloys, and coordination complexes of transplutonium elements under high pressure, summarizing key findings from the literature.
result: The review highlights the boundary between localized and itinerant 5f electrons in these materials and how pressure tunes their properties.
conclusion: Understanding transplutonium materials under pressure expands knowledge of heavy-element chemistry and physics, with implications for nuclear waste management and storage.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the quantum mechanical phenomena underlying low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, such as tunneling and resonances.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions at stellar energies is crucial for models of stellar burning and nucleosynthesis, but direct measurements are often impossible due to extremely small reaction rates.
method: The authors summarize the state-of-the-art theoretical approaches for low-energy nuclear reactions, including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discuss new experimental ideas.
result: The review provides a comprehensive overview of the quantum physics governing stellar nuclear reactions and highlights recent theoretical and experimental advances.
conclusion: Quantum mechanical effects are essential for describing stellar nuclear reactions, and continued theoretical and experimental efforts are needed to overcome the challenges of measuring these reactions at astrophysical energies.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants based on a least-squares adjustment of all available data.
motivation: Accurate and self-consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology, requiring periodic updates as new measurements become available.
method: A least-squares adjustment is performed on a global dataset of measurements and theoretical calculations, taking into account correlations and uncertainties to produce a consistent set of constant values.
result: The 2022 set of recommended values for fundamental constants and conversion factors is provided, with improved precision over previous editions.
conclusion: The CODATA recommended values serve as the internationally accepted standard for fundamental constants, supporting research and applications across physics and chemistry.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, covering single-particle and collective behaviors.
motivation: To unify the understanding of self-alignment in active systems and its implications for biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: Review of existing models and experimental observations, presenting a unified mathematical and conceptual framework.
result: Self-alignment enables novel behaviors such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental property that reshapes motion in active systems, with potential for groundbreaking applications.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed for biological and clinical insight; optoacoustic imaging offers high-resolution, deep-tissue optical contrast noninvasively.
method: The review discusses the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging of optical contrast at millimeter-to-centimeter depths with high resolution, and multimodal approaches enhance its capabilities.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical imaging, with ongoing developments in multimodal systems.

title: Wrinkles, Creases, And Cusps In Growing Soft Matter
authors: Martine Ben Amar
abstract:
Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

The buckling of a material surface subject to compression or growth is a ubiquitous phenomenon, arising in materials science contexts such as the swelling of gels as well as in biological contexts such as morphogenesis and embryogenesis. A complete understanding of the creases and sharp cusps that commonly accompany buckling requires nonlinear elasticity theory. This review presents a modern treatment of the Biot instability, integrating many standard techniques of nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, such as bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015004] Published Mon Feb 24, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nonlinear elasticity theory applied to buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding morphological instabilities in soft materials is important for materials science and biology, but the paper does not address quantum or information-theoretic aspects.
method: The review integrates techniques from nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, such as bifurcation theory and conformal mapping.
result: It provides a modern treatment of the Biot instability and related phenomena.
conclusion: The paper is a valuable resource for soft matter physics but falls outside the scope of the user's research interests.

motivation: Understanding the distribution of diffuse baryons in the cosmic web is a key goal in astrophysics, and FRBs provide a unique probe of ionized gas along their lines of sight.
method: The authors cross-correlate dispersion measures from the second CHIME/FRB catalog with galaxy positions from a spectroscopic survey, using a statistical estimator to extract the cross-power spectrum.
result: They detect a significant cross-correlation signal, demonstrating that FRB dispersion measures trace the large-scale structure traced by galaxies.
conclusion: This technique offers a new way to map the baryon distribution and constrain models of galaxy formation and the intergalactic medium.

method: The authors propose a paradigm that chases orbits instead of time, enabling efficient and accurate surrogate modeling of eccentric waveforms.
result: The method significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy, making eccentric templates feasible for routine gravitational-wave data analysis.
conclusion: This work enables the inclusion of eccentricity in gravitational-wave searches, improving astrophysical interpretation of detected signals.

It was quickly followed by work from the International Pulsar Timing Array (IPTA), demonstrating that the results of regiona…

motivation: Pulsar timing arrays have recently found evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background, but combining data from different arrays is challenging due to correlated noise and different array configurations.
method: The authors develop a Bayesian framework that models the common red noise process and uses a novel likelihood function to combine data from multiple PTAs, accounting for spatial correlations and noise properties.
result: The method improves the sensitivity to the gravitational wave background and provides a unified analysis of data from NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, and IPTA.
conclusion: The combined analysis yields stronger evidence for the gravitational wave background and better constraints on its spectrum, demonstrating the power of multi-array data combination.

[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 045201] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies radiation reaction effects on coherent emission in relativistic magnetized shocks, relevant to astrophysical fast radio bursts.
motivation: Understanding coherent radiation from relativistic shocks is key to explaining fast radio bursts, but radiation reaction effects on particle dynamics and emission have been underexplored.
method: The authors perform theoretical analysis and simulations of particle dynamics in magnetized shocks, incorporating radiation reaction forces.
result: Radiation reaction significantly alters particle trajectories and reduces the coherence of emitted radiation, impacting the predicted FRB properties.
conclusion: Radiation reaction must be accounted for in models of coherent emission from relativistic shocks to accurately interpret FRB observations.

motivation: Tungsten is a critical plasma-facing material in fusion reactors, and understanding radiation damage is essential for reactor design.
method: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations are used to model collision cascades and analyze defect production as a function of primary knock-on atom energy.
result: Four distinct regimes of primary damage are identified, including a linear regime at high energies, observed for the first time in silico.
conclusion: The results provide a comprehensive picture of radiation damage in tungsten, which can inform fusion reactor material design.

tldr: This essay discusses high-energy-density science, focusing on matter under extreme pressures and temperatures relevant to planetary interiors and fusion.
motivation: To explore the frontiers of high-energy-density physics and understand material behavior under extreme conditions.
method: Perspective article summarizing current knowledge and future directions in high-energy-density science.
result: Highlights the need for new experimental and theoretical approaches to study states of matter at extreme pressures and temperatures.
conclusion: High-energy-density science offers opportunities for discovery in planetary science, astrophysics, and fusion energy.

method: They use density matching to suppress sedimentation and field-induced alignment to counteract gyrotaxis, enabling electrokinetically driven active colloids to move in 3D.
result: The approach successfully facilitates sustained three-dimensional transport of active colloids in the bulk.
conclusion: Buoyancy control and external alignment can overcome sedimentation and gyrotaxis, allowing 3D active matter studies.

title: Dynamic Excitability Underlies Molluscan Shell Pigmentation
authors: P. S. Negi And E. Touber

Author(s): P. S. Negi and E. Touber

This work introduces a new class of excitable systems, which extends the well-known FitzHugh-Nagumo model to allow for dynamic variation of the phase sp…

result: They show that waves can both sustain and ultimately destroy large-scale 2D flows, explaining the energy transfer mechanism.
conclusion: The work provides a first-principles explanation for the dynamics of rotating turbulence, relevant to geophysical and astrophysical flows.

title: Colloquium: What Do We Mean By ‘active Matter’?
authors: Michael Te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, And Michael E. Cates
abstract:
Author(s): Michael te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, and Michael E. Cates

Active matter has become a lively topic in recent years, but what exactly is meant by the term ‘active matter’ is often unclear. This Colloquium discusses the scientific and semantic issues underlying this ambiguity, as well as the history of the field, and offers a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems. It then surveys recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 031001] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the definition, history, and recent developments of active matter, a subset of nonequilibrium systems.
motivation: The term 'active matter' is often used ambiguously; the paper aims to clarify its meaning and scope.
method: The authors review the history of the field, propose a definition, and survey recent topics including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.
result: A clear definition of active matter is provided, and its connections to other nonequilibrium phenomena are explored.
conclusion: Active matter is a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems with broad relevance, but the paper does not directly contribute to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: High-energy Emission From The Galactic Center
authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, and Régis Terrier

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy astrophysical emission from the Galactic Center, focusing on the supermassive black hole and surrounding structures.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength overview of the high-energy phenomena in the Galactic Center, which is the closest galactic nucleus and a unique laboratory for astrophysics.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths (X-ray, gamma-ray, etc.) and theoretical models of emission processes.
result: Summarizes the quiescent and flaring emission from Sgr A*, the properties of plasma bubbles and X-ray chimneys, and the interaction of cosmic rays with molecular clouds.
conclusion: The Galactic Center is a rich environment for studying high-energy astrophysics, with many open questions about particle acceleration and transport.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the interplay of surface defects, electric fields, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation and evolution.
result: A unified model emerges where tiny surface protrusions, field emission, Joule heating, and ion bombardment collectively trigger plasma formation.
conclusion: Recent advances provide a consistent understanding of vacuum breakdown, which can guide the design of more robust accelerator structures and other high-voltage vacuum systems.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: To understand strong interaction mechanisms such as quark confinement and gluon binding by studying charmonium decays and searching for new hadrons.
method: Review of experimental results from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments on hadron production in e+e- collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs.
result: Highlights recent advances from BESIII, which has become the leading facility for such measurements.
conclusion: The study of hadron production in charm-meson pairs provides valuable insights into QCD and hadron spectroscopy.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the scientific legacy of planetary radar observations at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids.
result: Arecibo's radar system was the most sensitive of its kind, enabling detailed characterization of many Solar System objects.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system made significant contributions to planetary science, and its loss is a major setback for the field.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A historical review of the Arecibo radio telescope's contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To document the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory and its impact on various fields of astronomy.
method: Historical narrative and review of key scientific achievements enabled by successive upgrades of the telescope.
result: Summarizes major contributions in pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave detection.
conclusion: Arecibo's upgrades continuously expanded its capabilities, leaving a lasting legacy in radio astronomy.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews geospace science advances made using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere have led to significant insights in plasma physics and space weather, but this work is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The paper is a colloquium review summarizing key results from incoherent scatter radar, lidar, and optical measurements of the ionosphere and magnetosphere.
result: It highlights advances in understanding ionospheric plasma physics, atomic metal layers, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in geospace research, but the paper does not contribute to the user's research interests in quantum information theory or related fields.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper discusses the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and their multimessenger implications.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper reviews detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and emphasizes simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It surveys potential implications for understanding physical and astrophysical processes in dense environments.
conclusion: Multimessenger observations with continuous gravitational waves will enhance our understanding of neutron star interiors and related physics.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm rain formation is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The authors review experimental, theoretical, and computational studies using convection-cloud chambers that reproduce key cloud processes under controlled conditions.
result: Convection-cloud chambers can capture turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentration and supersaturation, providing insights into the precipitation bottleneck.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales for understanding warm rain formation.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae, focusing on detection and parameter estimation.
motivation: Core collapse supernovae are rare events that provide unique multimessenger insights; detecting their gravitational waves is a key goal.
method: The paper summarizes recent supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection methods in ground-based interferometers.
result: It presents the latest progress in modeling and signal prediction, and outlines strategies for detection and parameter estimation.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from a nearby supernova would greatly advance understanding of the supernova engine and neutron star physics.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: Analysis failed

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, testing the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole in the large-scale matter distribution with the CMB dipole.
motivation: The cosmological principle is a foundational assumption of the standard ΛCDM model, and its validity can be tested by comparing the dipole anisotropy in galaxy catalogs with the CMB dipole.
method: The authors analyze recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in the matter distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole, accounting for potential biases and systematic effects.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, challenging the standard interpretation that the CMB dipole is due to our local peculiar motion.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may indicate a violation of the cosmological principle or require modifications to the ΛCDM model.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews astrophysical tests of self-interacting dark matter, focusing on dark matter halo dynamics and large-scale structure.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter by testing self-interaction models using astrophysical observations.
method: Review of theoretical predictions and observational constraints from galaxies to large-scale structures, within the Novel Probes Project.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and outlines future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable model, with ongoing and upcoming surveys expected to provide tighter constraints.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, but recent LHC results have constrained its parameter space. The paper aims to survey the current status and future discovery potential.
method: The authors review theoretical models and experimental search strategies, and project sensitivities for the High-Luminosity LHC across multiple channels.
result: The paper provides an overview of viable supersymmetric scenarios and estimates of discovery reach, but does not present new theoretical or experimental results.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable in certain regions, and the HL-LHC will significantly extend the search coverage, but no definitive conclusion on discovery is drawn.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion and neutrino production.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The review summarizes theoretical and experimental advances in nuclear reaction rates, plasma physics, and solar modeling.
result: Updated nuclear reaction rates and improved solar models are presented, with implications for neutrino fluxes and helioseismology.
conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive update on hydrogen-burning nuclear physics, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Nobel Lecture: Physics Is A Point Of View
authors: John J. Hopfield
abstract:
Author(s): John J. Hopfield

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030501] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Nobel lecture by John Hopfield reflecting on his career and the nature of physics.
motivation: To share personal insights and perspectives on physics as a field of inquiry.
method: Narrative and reflective lecture.
result: No novel research results; a retrospective on scientific discovery.
conclusion: Physics is a point of view that evolves with new discoveries and perspectives.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.

tldr: This Nobel lecture describes Boltzmann machines, a type of stochastic neural network for unsupervised learning.
motivation: To explain the principles and significance of Boltzmann machines in machine learning.
method: The lecture reviews the architecture, training algorithm (contrastive divergence), and connections to statistical physics.
result: Boltzmann machines can learn complex probability distributions and serve as generative models.
conclusion: Boltzmann machines are a foundational concept in deep learning, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding bubble dynamics is crucial for many natural and industrial processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review synthesizes advances over the past 20 years in bubble dynamics, focusing on fluid mechanics.
result: Key insights include the effects of added mass, deformable surfaces, turbulence, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive overview to guide future research in two-phase flow systems, but is unrelated to the user's research interests.
